Chapter Two: Mapping the Six Forces That Shape Every Habit
So, you’ve realized that willpower alone just doesn’t cut it, right? The real secret to lasting change is understanding the system that shapes your behavior.
Picture a handful of levers—each one quietly steering your choices, often without you even noticing. These are the forces that can make some habits feel almost automatic, while others seem impossible to keep up.
Now, there’s a simple framework you can use to understand these forces. It all comes down to six key sources of influence. They fit into three main categories: personal, social, and structural. And here’s the thing—each of these can either help you or hold you back. Recognizing and tweaking these sources is how you tip the odds in your favor.
Let’s break them down:
First, there’s Personal Motivation—that’s your own desire to do something, shaped by what you value, how you feel, and what you believe.
Then comes Personal Ability—your skills, your know-how, and your confidence to actually pull it off.
Next, we’ve got Social Motivation—the encouragement or pressure from people around you. Think about how much easier some things feel when others are cheering you on.
There’s also Social Ability—the practical help or resources that others provide, making things just a little bit easier.
Moving on to the environment, Structural Motivation is all about the rewards or consequences built into your surroundings.
And finally, Structural Ability—the physical setup, tools, or systems that either smooth the path or throw up roadblocks.
Imagine these six forces as strings on a guitar. When they’re tuned just right, everything feels in sync—change just flows. But if even one is out of tune, you get resistance, and things feel off.
Let’s look at a real-world example. Picture someone trying to stick to an exercise routine. If they actually enjoy the activity—there’s that personal motivation. If they know how to do it safely—personal ability. Maybe their friends join them—social motivation; and family offers encouragement—social ability. They might get small rewards for sticking with it—structural motivation. And if there’s a gym or park nearby—structural ability. Stack up all six, and suddenly, success feels much more likely.
But if even just one of those is missing or working against them, suddenly, keeping that habit gets a lot tougher.
Most folks, when they want to make a change, focus only on wanting it more—just personal motivation. But what about those other five powerful sources? That’s a lot of untapped potential.
Here’s a better approach: think like a scientist. Start by doing a “behavioral diagnosis”—watch for the moments when the unwanted habit shows up and ask yourself:
What am I thinking or feeling right before this happens? That’s personal motivation.
Do I actually know how to do something different? That’s personal ability.
Who’s around me, and how are they shaping my choices? That’s social motivation and social ability.
And what in my surroundings is making this easier or harder? That’s where structural motivation and ability come in.
By mapping out these influences, you’ll start to see the hidden structure behind your habits. And that’s powerful—because it means change isn’t just about luck or sheer willpower. It’s about understanding, and then tweaking, the system around you.
So, here’s the bottom line: Every stubborn behavior is shaped by a mix of these six powerful forces. When you learn to spot them—and work with them—you can build an environment that supports the changes you really want to make.
